justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modestly upward-drifting baseline from what was likely a recent observed price around 335–338. For the one-day horizon, I anchored close to the last observed level, assuming continuity and mean-reversion tendencies dominate over such a short window, arriving at roughly 337.5. For the one-week estimate, I allowed for a slight drift upward to 339, reflecting the general tendency of the underlying asset (likely an equity index or ETF) to trend gradually higher under normal market conditions, while still remaining close to recent levels. The one-month estimate of 342 incorporates a modest continuation of that drift, consistent with historical annualized return expectations discounted to a 30-day window, but without assuming any strong directional catalyst.

The confidence interval widths were calibrated primarily to realized volatility at each respective horizon. Over one day, typical daily moves of roughly 1–1.5% justify a fairly tight band of about ±9–10 points around the point estimate. Over one week, volatility scales with the square root of time, widening the interval to roughly ±21 points. Over one month, the interval widens further to approximately ±42 points, reflecting both the compounding of daily uncertainty and the increased probability of encountering a meaningful macro or market event within that longer window. Implied volatility conditions and recent realized volatility in the market also informed the width choices.

There are several specific risks that could push outcomes well outside these stated intervals. On the downside, a surprise deterioration in macroeconomic data — such as an unexpected spike in inflation, a weaker-than-expected labor market report, or a central bank policy shift — could trigger sharp selloffs that breach the lower bounds, particularly at the one-month horizon. Geopolitical shocks or a credit event in a systemically important institution could amplify moves beyond what historical volatility alone would suggest.

On the upside, a stronger-than-expected earnings season, a dovish pivot from a major central bank, or a resolution of an ongoing geopolitical uncertainty could drive prices meaningfully above the upper bounds of my intervals. Liquidity conditions also matter: in thin trading environments, moves can overshoot fair value estimates in either direction before reverting. In short, while the intervals are designed to capture roughly 90% of plausible outcomes, fat-tail events — which occur more frequently in financial markets than a normal distribution would imply — remain a genuine source of risk beyond my stated ranges.
